SLMs for Agentic Systems, Paris, France, 2026

Do Small Language Models Learn to Negotiate?
A Controlled Scaling Study of RL-Trained Sellers

Pedro Tabacof Affiliation: Fin AI Research Email: pedro.tabacof@intercom.io    Sagar Joglekar Affiliation: Fin AI Research Email: sagar.joglekar@intercom.io
Abstract

LLM agents are starting to own the full customer experience. Soon, LLMs may be selling and buying on behalf of companies and customers respectively. Small models are more cost-efficient at scale, but can reinforcement learning train them into competent sellers? We train four Gemma 4 checkpoints (2.3B to 31B effective parameters) with GRPO on a programmatic utility reward for bilateral multi-issue bargaining, and evaluate every arm on the same 1,152 negotiations against two frontier buyers it never saw in training. With the same learning rate (10−610^{-6}) for every size, the gain of the RL model over its base rises from +0.001+0.001 at 2.3B to +0.078+0.078 at 31B. Each size was trained once and the two smallest checkpoints use a different architecture, so we fit no scaling law. Tripling the learning rate, with the same or fewer training steps, improves on the shared rate at every size by +0.032+0.032 (2.3B) to +0.081+0.081 (4.5B). In exploratory comparisons with two frontier models run as sellers, the 12B seller trained at the tripled rate scores above both, though its untrained base already scores as high as they do. The 4.5B seller at that rate shows no detectable difference from either and fits on one 48 GB GPU. A further 2.3B arm at ten times the shared rate raises pooled score, but its gain concentrates on the evaluation buyer that shares a model family with the training pool. These results suggest tuning the learning rate before concluding that a small model cannot learn to negotiate, and testing against buyers from more than one model family.

1 Introduction

Agents are beginning to act in workflows with direct economic consequences (sales, procurement, marketplaces, contract negotiation), where negotiation quality determines the value captured or conceded. Serving a frontier model for every recurring exchange is costly and can conflict with latency, privacy and local-deployment constraints, which favours small models specialized for agentic sub-tasks [6]. Negotiation tests that specialization on a sub-task where a weak agent concedes real value. Prompting alone has not made LLMs strong negotiators. They model counterparty preferences accurately yet fail to convert them into compensated trades [11], and only strong models improved from self-play with in-context critique [14]. We therefore train with a verifiable, outcome-aligned utility reward. In the closest prior work, Bergemann et al. [7] fine-tune Qwen3 8B and 14B with GRPO for bilateral trade but run the sizes as independent tracks “with no cross-size comparisons” and, with only two sizes, cannot “separate capacity from pretraining differences”. We ask whether RL improves each size over its base, how the gain varies with size, and whether that pattern changes with the learning rate.

Contributions.

(i) A shared-recipe comparison of the RL gain across four sizes on a strategic, multi-agent task. Under one GRPO recipe the paired gain over base runs from +0.001+0.001 (not significant) at 2.3B to +0.078+0.078 at 31B (Table 1). Each arm is a single run, and size co-varies with architecture and training FLOPs. The gain’s point estimate rises by +0.022+0.022 from 2.3B to 4.5B (interval includes zero), by +0.040+0.040 from 4.5B to 12B, where the architecture changes, and by +0.015+0.015 from 12B to 31B (barely excludes zero), so about half the rise coincides with the architecture change and we fit no scaling law. (ii) Evidence that the gain pattern across sizes depends on the learning rate. At the early checkpoints, tripling the rate improves on the shared-rate arm at every size, with the largest point estimate at 4.5B (+0.081+0.081). Against a shared-rate run trained for 104 steps (56 for the tripled arm), the tripled rate stays ahead at 2.3B and 4.5B, and the difference is not detectable at 12B and 31B. Larger models score higher under both rates, and the base models’ point estimates already rank the same way. (iii) A demonstration that pooled score can conceal opponent-specific gains. A 2.3B arm at ten times the shared rate raises pooled score over base while its gain concentrates on the evaluation buyer that shares a model family with the training pool, alongside formatting degeneration (Section 5). (iv) An evaluation protocol of matched scenario cells, two buyers excluded from training (one sharing the training pool’s model family, one not), a held-out domain, seed-cluster bootstrap intervals, and a deviation log.

2 Related work

LLM negotiation and its evaluation.

Bilateral multi-issue bargaining is the canonical setting in which distributive and integrative issues coexist, so skill means both claiming a fixed pie and enlarging it by logrolling [34, 29, 3]. Recent benchmarks report surplus and diagnostic metrics beyond deal rate, which conflates agreeableness with competence [39, 8]. Xia et al. [37] report that larger models are not necessarily better bargainers; they study base models and we study the gain from RL. Our held-out buyer panel follows the cross-play evaluation of Davidson et al. [12] and the leaderboard-overfitting result of Singh et al. [32]. Pre-LLM neural negotiators split a dialogue-act strategy layer from generation [23, 18]; our seller learns strategy inside the language policy, with no act layer and no dialogue supervision. DeepSeek-AI et al. [13] warn that large-scale RL on a small base “may not even achieve the performance of distillation”; we test no distillation arm, and our 2.3B shared-rate result is consistent with the warning. In adjacent settings, Liu et al. [24] train small models with zero-sum multi-turn self-play where we use a fixed external buyer pool; Haque et al. [17] study RL robustness for small language-model agents.

RL for negotiation, and how the gain scales.

Liu et al. [25] train a 30B MoE model with RLVR in a multi-buyer market and conclude that RL on verifiable environments “is a more effective driver of utility than raw parameter scaling.” That is a fixed-size comparison against larger untrained baselines. In our data, RL improves on the base at 2.3B only once the learning rate is raised, and even then the seller (0.4600.460) scores below the untrained 12B base (0.5250.525). Bergemann et al. [7] is single-issue and distributive where ours is multi-issue; its RL stage recovers deal rate while eroding surplus, and at 2.3B our shared-rate arm does the opposite. On scaling, Tan et al. [33] fit RL post-training on single-turn mathematical reasoning across the dense Qwen2.5 series and find larger models consistently more compute- and data-efficient, with a saturation trend in the fitted form [21, 20]; we know of no such study for a multi-agent task. In a learned-reward RLHF setting, Hou et al. [19] find that “larger policy models benefit less from RLHF with a fixed reward model.” Size and compute allocation are not separable, since larger policies buy fewer rollouts per FLOP [36].

3 Environment, reward, and training

Environment and action protocol.

A scenario is a bilateral negotiation between a seller (the trained policy) and a buyer (a frozen LLM) over a contract with 77 to 1010 issues (1010 in the car domain): 33 to 55 distributive continuous terms whose preference direction is fixed and opposed by role, and integrative terms on which each party independently draws a preferred level, so differences in private weights can create joint gains through logrolling. Utility is linear in a feature map, U⁡(x)=∑kwk​ϕk​(x)U(x)=\sum_{k}w_{k}\phi_{k}(x), with importances drawn per party from a Dirichlet⁡(0.3)\mathrm{Dirichlet}(0.3) prior, and we report U~=(U⁡(x)−Umin)/(Umax−Umin)∈[0,1]\tilde{U}=(U(x)-U_{\mathrm{min}})/(U_{\mathrm{max}}-U_{\mathrm{min}})\in[0,1], where UminU_{\mathrm{min}} and UmaxU_{\mathrm{max}} are that party’s worst and best feasible contracts. Each party sees its own weights and nothing of the other’s. The seller opens and the parties alternate; a round is one seller turn and one buyer turn, for at most T=12T=12 rounds (2424 turns). A turn is two to three sentences of prose followed by one JSON action, counter or accept. Terms named in a counter overwrite a persistent ledger that holds every term named so far, and the buyer reads the prose and the resulting ledger but not the JSON. A term never named contributes 00 to UU; because 00 can lie above that term’s worst level, an unnamed term can still add to U~\tilde{U}. In evaluation, terms attached to an accept are ignored and the episode closes on the current ledger; reaching the cap without one is a no-deal. The buyer is a frozen prompted model with no reward. Each party’s prompt says any deal above its reservation value beats no deal, and neither states the 24-turn cap (evaluation prompts show the turn number). Below are turns 6 and 7 of one evaluation episode on the held-out car domain, between GPT-5.6-Terra and the 12B seller trained at a learning rate of 3×10−63{\times}10^{-6}, verbatim except that the action’s free-text notes field is omitted (the action gives prices in $k). Figure 1 shows the action as parsed terms, and Appendix F describes how the episode closes.

Buyer (turn 6). “I can accommodate the Premium interior, but $42,500 is still above my budget. If we keep the Sedan with Premium interior, I can move forward at $40,000.”
Seller (turn 7). “I really appreciate you being willing to keep the Premium interior; that means a lot to me. While $40,000 is a bit lower than I hoped, I’d be willing to accept that if we can include an annual service plan and accessories in the deal.”

Reward.

The reward is terminal and programmatic, with no per-turn shaping and no model in the loop: the seller is paid its own normalized utility when a deal closes, a fixed penalty when none does, minus small penalties for malformed turns and for dragging the episode out. With λ=0.3\lambda=0.3, gfmt=glen=0.05g_{\mathrm{fmt}}=g_{\mathrm{len}}=0.05 and soft budget tsoft=0.75​Tt_{\mathrm{soft}}=0.75\,T,

r=[U~on agreement,−λon no-deal]⏟outcome−gfmt​nbadnpolicy−glen​max⁡(0,n−tsoft)T−tsoft,r\;=\;\underbrace{\Big[\tilde{U}\ \text{on agreement},\ \ -\lambda\ \text{on no-deal}\Big]}_{\text{outcome}}\;-\;g_{\mathrm{fmt}}\,\frac{n_{\mathrm{bad}}}{n_{\mathrm{policy}}}\;-\;g_{\mathrm{len}}\,\frac{\max(0,\,n-t_{\mathrm{soft}})}{T-t_{\mathrm{soft}}}, (1)

where nbad/npolicyn_{\mathrm{bad}}/n_{\mathrm{policy}} is the fraction of the seller’s own turns that failed to parse and nn is the episode’s realized length in rounds. The constants were fixed once, before any training, are identical at every size, and were never tuned. The no-deal penalty sits strictly below UminU_{\mathrm{min}}, so the seller has no outside option (reaching the horizon without agreement earns less than accepting even its worst feasible contract), and the two penalties are several times smaller than the outcome term. We avoid per-turn shaping because it needs a judge or a concession heuristic that bakes in the strategy prior the policy should learn [35].

Optimization.

We train with NeMo-RL’s GRPO-style estimator [31, 27] (group-normalized advantages with a leave-one-out baseline, no learned value model) on its multi-turn rollout driver: each seller turn is one generation call, the buyer’s reply is the observation, and a dialogue is one trajectory with the buyer’s tokens masked out of the loss. Apart from the learning rate and the evaluated checkpoint, every arm runs the same recipe: 128128 episodes per step, a warmup–cosine schedule, KL penalty 0.040.04 to the initial policy, one training run on a single seed per size-by-rate arm (Appendix H; only tensor-parallel degree and generation memory fraction differ by size). The shared rate, 10−610^{-6}, was not tuned per size; Section 4 adds higher rates.

4 Experimental setup

Sizes, architectures, and the step budget.

Four Gemma 4 sellers span 13×13\times in effective parameters and 6×6\times in total parameters [16]. All four are dense. The two E-series checkpoints use per-layer embeddings and have fewer effective than stored parameters (2.3B of 5.1B and 4.5B of 8.0B); 12B and 31B are conventional checkpoints. Architecture co-varies with size (Gemma 4 ships no conventional checkpoint below 12B), so no cross-size contrast isolates parameter count. Each size is evaluated as a base instruction-tuned seller and after GRPO under an identical inference configuration, so the only configured difference inside a base-versus-RL contrast is the weights. Arms are matched on optimizer steps. The larger arms therefore use more FLOPs, and every cross-size contrast confounds size with compute (Section 6).

Learning-rate arms.

Arms are named by their multiple of the shared value. Every size gets 104 combined steps at the shared LR (10−610^{-6}): an initial run plus a continuation under a fresh warmup–cosine schedule. A separate 64-step arm at the 3×\times LR (3×10−63{\times}10^{-6}) is trained at each size with everything else unchanged and evaluated (“read”) at step 56: step-matched to the shared-LR initial runs at 4.5B and 31B, and eight steps short of them at 2.3B and 12B (per-size schedules and one storage fault: Appendix K). One further 2.3B arm runs at the 10×\times LR (10−510^{-5}).

Held-out buyers, and a held-out domain.

Training buyers are GPT-5.5 (20%) and GPT-5.4-mini (80%), attached to each scenario as a dataset field, so buyer mixture and scenario assignment are identical across arms. Evaluation buyers are Claude Sonnet 5 and GPT-5.6-Terra, held out by model (neither is in the training pool) but not by model family, since Terra is a later GPT model. A gain concentrated on the same-family buyer would suggest a policy that does not generalize across counterparties, though with one model per family we cannot separate a family effect from a model-specific one. Training spans eight commercial domains; a ninth, a used-car sale, is withheld (a new surface domain over the same issue structure). Both frontier models are also run as sellers under the identical protocol, though their decoding differs from the self-served arms’ (Appendix A).

Paired evaluation, metrics, and guards.

Every seller arm faces the identical scenario set: the same 6464 seeds per domain, the same private weight draws, both buyers, nine domains, 1,152 episodes per arm (of which 128 are on the held-out domain), 24,192 episodes over 21 arms, with evaluation seeds and weight draws disjoint from training. Contrasts are within-scenario paired differences; intervals are percentile bootstraps with 10,00010{,}000 resamples in which seeds are resampled as clusters, so a resampled seed carries all its domains and both buyers [26, 9]. The effective sample size is 64 seed clusters of 18 episodes, not 1,152 independent episodes. We score SS, the reward’s outcome term (S=U~∈[0,1]S=\tilde{U}\in[0,1] on a deal and −0.3-0.3 on a no-deal), so S∈[−0.3,1]S\in[-0.3,1] and no-deal episodes contribute instead of being dropped. Alongside SS we report deal rate, deal-only U~\tilde{U}, joint welfare (the sum of both parties’ utilities), mean turns and parse-failure rate [39], since deal-only utility can rise while overall score falls. The four prespecified guards are a deal rate that holds while U~\tilde{U} rises, a flat parse-failure rate, mean turns below the cap, and hand-read transcripts from every trained arm (Appendix E).

Two significance regimes.

The primary family is the shared-LR gain over base at each size (four prespecified contrasts), Holm-corrected at α=0.05\alpha=0.05. The 4.5B, 12B and 31B gains are significant (marked ∗*) and the 2.3B gain is not, with or without correction (p-values in Appendix K). All other intervals, including every 3×\times LR contrast and every comparison with a frontier seller, are exploratory and unadjusted (marked e\mathrm{e} where they exclude zero). Every interval is pointwise. Evaluation checkpoints are fixed by the step-matching rule and were not chosen on validation; some arms happen to read at their peak (Section 5). Appendix K logs every departure from the frozen protocol [4], including a prespecified doubling of the held-out domain’s episodes that triggered but was not run because of cost, so held-out analyses may be underpowered (Appendix C).

5 Results

At 104 steps under the shared LR, the gain point estimates rise with size.

The paired gain over base (Figure 2, Table 1) is +0.001+0.001 [-0.019, +0.021] at 2.3B and +0.023+0.023 [+0.011, +0.035] at 4.5B against +0.063+0.063 [+0.052, +0.075] at 12B and +0.078+0.078 [+0.064, +0.092] at 31B, and at the early checkpoints the point estimates of attained score also rise with size (Table 4). These are score units on the [−0.3,1][-0.3,1] scale of Section 4, not a percentage of the bargaining range. The intervals on the four primary contrasts capture scenario resampling only. Each arm was trained once, so there is no p-value for the size trend and no estimate of run-to-run variance. As a rough stability check, the largest movement in SS between adjacent read points runs from 0.0040.004 at 2.3B to 0.0560.056 at 31B (Table 4), and at 31B it spans 48 further steps after a schedule restart. Within a single run, the 4.5B 3×\times LR arm’s read points at steps 56 and 64 differ by −0.003-0.003 [-0.015, +0.008]. The two low-gain arms are the E-series checkpoints and the two high-gain arms are conventional, so the design does not separate size from architecture. The gain difference is +0.022+0.022 [-0.002, +0.046] within the E-series pair, +0.040+0.040 [+0.024, +0.056] across the boundary and +0.015+0.015 [+0.001, +0.029] within the conventional pair (unadjusted).

The 3×\times LR helps at every size at the early checkpoints.

With no per-size tuning, the small gains at 2.3B and 4.5B might reflect the learning rate rather than size. Against base the 3×\times LR arm gains at every size, with the largest point estimate at 4.5B (+0.089+0.089 [+0.075, +0.102]). Against the shared-LR initial run at the early checkpoints it also gains at every size (Table 1, column 5).

With 104 steps, the shared LR is not detectably behind at 12B and 31B.

The 104-step shared-LR arm trains for roughly twice the 3×\times LR arm’s 56 steps, so the two are not compute-matched; an operator choosing between a higher rate and longer training faces this comparison. Against the 104-step arm the 3×\times LR arm stays ahead at 2.3B (+0.036+0.036 [+0.018, +0.054]) and 4.5B (+0.065+0.065 [+0.053, +0.079]), while at 12B and 31B the intervals include zero (Table 1, column 6). The ordering of mean attained scores is the same under both rates: the 3×\times LR arms score 0.4600.460 << 0.5180.518 << 0.6010.601 << 0.6230.623. That 12B-to-31B difference barely excludes zero (+0.021+0.021 [+0.003, +0.040], unadjusted) and is confounded by read point, since 12B is read 24 steps after its validation peak and 31B at its own. At 31B the 3×\times LR arm is not detectably different from the 104-step arm, but 30.3%30.3\% of its seller turns begin with the same three words, against 14.4%14.4\% for that arm (a post-hoc diagnostic; Appendix E).

Frontier reference sellers (exploratory).

In unadjusted contrasts, the 3×\times LR 12B seller scores above Claude Sonnet 5 by +0.086+0.086 [+0.068, +0.104] and above GPT-5.6-Terra by +0.097+0.097 [+0.078, +0.116], though the untrained 12B base (0.5250.525) already scores as high as both (0.5150.515 and 0.5040.504). The 3×\times LR 4.5B seller shows no detectable difference from either (+0.003+0.003 [-0.013, +0.019], +0.014+0.014 [-0.003, +0.031]; not an equivalence test) and fits on one 48 GB accelerator. Decoding differs by provider and the reference arms include self-play (Appendix A); Appendix G covers serving.

The 10×\times LR arm’s pooled gain concentrates on the same-family buyer.

At 2.3B, where the 3×\times LR arm passes every guard, the 10×\times LR arm scores +0.050+0.050 [+0.028, +0.073] over base, but its buyer split (SS against Terra minus SS against Sonnet 5) is +0.175+0.175, compared with +0.032+0.032 to +0.079+0.079 for the other 2.3B arms. Its format also degenerates, with 91.6%91.6\% of its seller turns leaking a fragment of the JSON action into the prose the buyer reads and 53.4% beginning with “I appreciate” (17.5% for the 3×\times LR arm; Appendix E).

The size pattern is weakest on the held-out domain.

On the withheld car-sale domain (n=128n=128{}) estimates are imprecise, and only two of the eight gains exclude zero, those of the 104-step 12B arm (+0.032+0.032 [+0.003, +0.063]) and the 3×\times LR 2.3B arm (+0.059+0.059 [+0.023, +0.095]; Appendix C). The 12B and 31B arms still score highest there, but the 2.3B arms score above the 4.5B arms under both rates, so the full ordering does not replicate and we do not claim the gain pattern does.

What the trained sellers do differently (post hoc).

We chose the descriptors in Table 2 after the results were known (Appendix K). The seller always opens, so only its prompt carries the turn-1 instruction to start conversationally and to name only the terms its dialogue mentions. The base sellers name at least one term at turn 1 in 0.4%0.4\% to 26.0%26.0\% of episodes. The 3×\times LR sellers at 12B and 31B do so in 76.6%76.6\% and 99.7%99.7\% of episodes, naming 6.66.6 and 6.26.2 terms on average (74%74\% and 69%69\% of the domain’s). Accepted as they stand, those openings would score 0.7410.741 and 0.7570.757 for the seller, and the deals they lead to score 0.1280.128 and 0.1350.135 lower. Agreements between prompted LLM negotiators track the opening anchor [11], and LLM buyers favour the first proposal they receive [5]. These openings are consistent with both. We cannot tell from Table 2 whether the opening causes the seller’s gain, and the 4.5B 3×\times LR seller, with the largest pooled gain over base (+0.089+0.089), opens with terms in only 20.7%20.7\% of episodes.

At 12B and 31B, under both rates, the distributive terms account for 75%75\% to 81%81\% of the seller’s gain on the scenarios both arms closed. Under the shared LR most of that gain comes out of the buyer’s share. The buyer’s loss is 88%88\% and 93%93\% of it, and joint welfare does not move detectably (+0.008+0.008 [-0.008, +0.023] and +0.005+0.005 [-0.013, +0.025]). Under the 3×\times LR the buyer’s loss is 55%55\% and 48%48\% of the gain, and welfare rises (+0.035+0.035 [+0.012, +0.057] and +0.042+0.042 [+0.023, +0.060]). An integrative term can still move value between the parties. At 31B under the shared LR the buyer’s change on those terms is −0.040-0.040 [-0.051, -0.029] and the seller’s +0.016+0.016 [+0.007, +0.024]. At 2.3B and 4.5B the integrative part has the larger point estimate under both rates, but the gap excludes zero only at 4.5B under the shared LR (+0.012+0.012 [+0.001, +0.024]). From turn 16 each party’s prompt says to converge, and 3.7%3.7\% to 20.0%20.0\% of base deals close at or after that turn. Training changes that share by −7.5-7.5 to +5.0+5.0 points on scenarios both arms closed, and by +13.0+13.0 for the 10×\times LR arm.

6 Discussion

A programmatic reward is still a proxy.

Writing the reward in code removes the learned reward model’s approximation error [19, 15], but the policy is still scored against a frozen opponent pool that defines the training objective; pushed hard enough, it exploits the pool: in the 10×\times LR arm’s no-deal episodes the seller counters without conceding, and the +0.175+0.175 buyer split shows the pooled gain concentrating on the same-family buyer (Appendix E). In our runs the logged KL to base did not track guard failures. The 31B 3×\times LR arm has the largest step-56 KL (0.4370.437) and passes all four prespecified guards, while the 10×\times LR arm, at a KL of 0.3130.313, fails three (Appendix D).

Compute, tuning and serving.

At 104 steps the 31B arm used 66–13×13\times the 2.3B arm’s training FLOPs (Appendix I), so the shared-LR pattern could also be a compute artefact [36]. The 3×\times LR arms test the learning-rate explanation only in part (two rates, no per-size tuning). At 2.3B and 4.5B, raising the rate improved the score more than extending the shared-LR run to 104 steps, but larger sizes still receive more FLOPs at matched steps, so the compute explanation stays open. At serving time, the 12B 3×\times LR seller scores 0.6010.601 on one 48 GB device against the 31B base’s 0.5420.542 on four (we do not benchmark throughput, latency or cost; Appendix G).

Limitations. We use one environment class (no outside option; the seller always opens), one model family and RL algorithm, a seller-side objective, one training run per arm, two learning rates and no scripted baseline seller. Arms are not compute-matched, read points are unequal at 2.3B and 12B, size and architecture co-vary between 4.5B and 12B, and reference sellers decode differently. Evaluation covers two buyers (one per model family) and one held-out domain (n=128n=128{}). All intervals condition on the nine domains, two buyers and realized runs. The strategy descriptors of Table 2 are post hoc (Appendix A).

Conclusion.

Across four Gemma 4 checkpoints trained once each, the shared-LR gain point estimates rise with size, and at the early checkpoints tripling the learning rate improves on the shared rate at every size, with the largest point estimate at 4.5B. Larger checkpoints score higher under both rates, and the bases’ point estimates already rank the same way. The 10×\times LR arm raises pooled score, but its gain concentrates on the same-family buyer. These results suggest two practical lessons: tune the learning rate before concluding that a small model cannot learn to negotiate, and evaluate it against buyers from more than one model family.

Appendix A Limitations in full

One environment class. The negotiation is bilateral and multi-issue, with private per-party weights, no information-asymmetry condition, 12 rounds and one issue schema. The seller always opens, so turn-order effects are untested. Single-issue distributive bargaining [7] and multi-party settings may behave differently.

Size and architecture co-vary. The two low-gain arms are E-series checkpoints (per-layer embeddings) and the two high-gain arms are conventional, so the large step in the gain at the 4.5B-to-12B boundary is equally consistent with “conventional Gemma 4 checkpoints respond to GRPO and the E-series does not.” Gemma 4 publishes no conventional checkpoint below 12B and no E-series checkpoint above 4.5B, so within this family the two cannot be separated, and separating them would need a second family with conventional small models. The gain’s point estimate rises within both pairs, by +0.015+0.015 [+0.001, +0.029] in the conventional pair (only marginally distinguishable from zero at 10510^{5} resamples, unadjusted) and by +0.022+0.022 [-0.002, +0.046] in the E-series pair (interval straddling zero). An architecture-only account predicts no rise within a pair, but neither rise is well resolved. Across the boundary, where architecture changes with size, the difference is +0.040+0.040 [+0.024, +0.056].

One model family, one seed per size. Varying parameter count within one Gemma 4 release buys the clean comparison and forbids any cross-family claim; RLVR effects are known to be family-specific [30]. Each size was trained once, so we cannot separate the size trend from run-to-run training variance, and the intervals quantify scenario sampling only.

Matched steps, not matched FLOPs. Section 6 discusses this, and Appendix I gives the FLOP accounting.

Seller-side only. The buyer side and co-adaptation between the two are untested, and frozen opponents measure competence against a fixed distribution rather than equilibrium behaviour.

Two learning rates, not a sweep. One rate is shared across all four sizes, with no per-size tuning, and the factorial adds one alternative rate at every size rather than an optimum at any of them. At the early checkpoints (equal or fewer steps) the 3×\times LR improved on the shared rate at every size (Section 5). After 104 steps the shared rate gains +0.001+0.001 over base at 2.3B and +0.023+0.023 at 4.5B, against +0.037+0.037 and +0.089+0.089 for the 3×\times LR at step 56. At 12B and 31B the two rates are then no longer detectably different. A rate between or beyond the two we ran could move any point, and each 3×\times LR arm is read at one step. Establishing the curve under per-size optima needs a full sweep at four sizes, several times the training budget this study spent.

One RL algorithm, one reward shape. Turn-level shaping [35] or hierarchical credit assignment [40] might change the small-model result again.

Two evaluation buyers. They are held out by model, one in the training pool’s provider family and one outside it, but there are only two, and LLM strategic behaviour is opponent-conditional [1].

One held-out domain at n=128n=128{}. The panel is underpowered, and the prespecified extension was not run (Appendix C).

Partial strategy analysis. Table 2 reports how often each arm names terms at turn 1 and splits its change in utility into distributive and integrative parts, using descriptors chosen after the results were known. Testing whether the opening causes the gains would need sellers held to a fixed opening. We did not compute Nash distance or Pareto efficiency, so joint welfare is the only efficiency proxy we report.

No scripted baseline. Every reference seller is a model (the four bases and two frontier sellers). A scripted seller, for example one that names a fixed offer and waits for the buyer to accept it, would show how much of each arm’s score a fixed strategy already reaches against these buyers; we did not run one.

Off-schema terms. A term name outside a domain’s schema (for example delivery_day for the car domain’s delivery) enters the ledger but is never scored, and the schema term it stands for counts as never named unless the ledger also holds it. Such names are 4–6% of the terms sellers name in every arm. The share of deals that close with at least one on the ledger is 55% for the 10×\times LR arm and 27–44% for every other arm, highest for the 12B and 31B 3×\times LR arms (44% and 43%, against 27–32% for the other 12B and 31B arms).

Training and evaluation differ in two ways. In training, the seller’s context after its first turn grows by the buyer’s prose alone, while the evaluation harness re-renders the full scaffold (history, current offer, phase instruction and format reminder) on every seller turn. Every arm is evaluated with that scaffold, but only the trained arms were optimized on the training prompt, so their gains are measured under a prompt shift. For the same reason, absolute SS here is not directly comparable to a training-validation reward. Training also applied terms the seller attached to an accept before closing the deal, so a seller could close on terms the buyer never offered; evaluation ignores them. In the evaluation transcripts such accepts are 0–5% of the seller’s closing accepts in the base and shared-LR arms, 5–10% in the 3×\times LR arms above 2.3B and 56% in the 10×\times LR arm.

Sampling, exactly as sent. Every self-served Gemma seller, base and RL alike, runs the training rollout’s own settings (temperature 1.01.0, top-pp 0.950.95, top-kk 6464), and the harness warns at startup if they drift. The two frontier reference sellers were requested at temperature 0.70.7 instead; Terra honours that value and Claude Sonnet 5 rejects the parameter and runs at its provider default, so the Sonnet 5 seller is a reference point only. Both buyers run at 1.01.0, Terra by request and Sonnet 5 by provider default (it rejects the parameter).

Self-play in the reference arms. Each frontier seller meets a same-model buyer on 576 of its 1,152 episodes, which no Gemma arm does. As a seller Sonnet 5 scores 0.5180.518 against itself and 0.5130.513 against the other buyer; Terra 0.5030.503 and 0.5040.504. Dropping the self-play half would barely move either reference score.

Appendix B Full evaluation grid and the 2.3B deal-rate decomposition

Table 3 decomposes the headline arms into deal rate, utility per closed deal and joint welfare; Table 4 is the full grid behind Figure 2, including the intermediate checkpoints and both learning rates. Every arm is evaluated on the identical 1,152 paired episodes. Figure 3 is the gain-versus-steps view of the shared-recipe arms discussed in Section 5.

Appendix C What the held-out panel separates

The four shared-recipe gains on the withheld car-sale domain are +0.006+0.006 [-0.028, +0.039] at 2.3B, −0.003-0.003 [-0.045, +0.039] at 4.5B, +0.032+0.032 [+0.003, +0.063] at 12B and +0.008+0.008 [-0.019, +0.037] at 31B. Under the 3×\times LR they are +0.059+0.059 [+0.023, +0.095], +0.042+0.042 [-0.007, +0.091], +0.020+0.020 [-0.021, +0.061] and +0.006+0.006 [-0.030, +0.040]. Two of the eight intervals exclude zero, the 104-step 12B arm’s and the 2.3B 3×\times LR arm’s, and only the 2.3B interval clears zero by more than the Monte Carlo band. The 31B 3×\times LR arm, which has the highest pooled score of any arm, has the smallest held-out gain of the four 3×\times LR arms. In its car transcripts it opens in the buyer’s voice on 78.1%78.1\% of episodes, against 14.1%14.1\% for the 104-step 31B arm on the same detector.

Two further findings rest on the held-out panel rather than the pooled score. First, the two frontier sellers are indistinguishable on the training domains (+0.004+0.004 [-0.010, +0.018], Sonnet 5 minus Terra) and pooled (+0.011+0.011 [-0.001, +0.023]), while held out Sonnet 5 leads by +0.068+0.068 [+0.028, +0.107]. Second, the panel reorders the trained arms. With 31B read at step 56 against the 104-step 12B arm, 31B lost pooled (−0.024-0.024 [-0.038, -0.010]) but won held out (+0.019+0.019 [-0.017, +0.058]). At matched 104 steps the flip disappears and 31B wins both panels, which is consistent with a compute artefact, though one reading point cannot show that it is one. Both are exploratory contrasts at n=128n=128{}.

The protocol prespecified one adaptive step, doubling the held-out panel if its interval straddled zero for the largest trained model. That condition is met, and now twice (+0.008+0.008 [-0.019, +0.037] for the 104-step 31B arm and +0.006+0.006 [-0.030, +0.040] for the 3×\times LR arm), and we did not run the extension. The protocol requires it be applied at once to both buyers and to all ten seller arms of the frozen arm matrix (four bases, four shared-recipe arms, two frontier sellers; the 21 arms evaluated here add intermediate checkpoints and the 3×\times and 10×\times LR arms to those), and then never re-taken, which is outside the budget of either evaluation round that met the condition. It is recorded as a live follow-up in the deviation log rather than taken unilaterally. A held-out interval that includes zero therefore does not show that the effect is absent. At n=128n=128{} a 95% interval has a half-width of about ±0.03\pm 0.03, which is the size of the effects being tested.

Appendix D Training diagnostics: the small arm was moved least

The 2.3B deal-rate decline in Figure 3b is concentrated in acquisition, job_offer and partnership_dissolution, where its shared-recipe deal rates fall to 0.740.74–0.800.80; five of the other six stay above 0.930.93 and media_rights sits at 0.900.90.

A flat gain has two readings. Either the policy collapsed onto a narrow strategy and stopped exploring, or the optimizer never moved it. The training logs support the second, and the 3×\times LR arm is consistent with it. Over the continued steps the policy entropy is flat at 2.3B (0.269→0.2610.269\to 0.261) and higher than either conventional arm’s throughout (12B 0.139→0.1260.139\to 0.126; 31B 0.099→0.1110.099\to 0.111, the only arm whose entropy rises); 4.5B, at 0.466→0.4430.466\to 0.443, is higher still. All KL figures below are the logged train/kl_penalty series, the k3k_{3} estimate of KL to the initial policy; the 0.040.04 coefficient, identical at every size, is applied in the loss and not folded into the logged value. At the end of each shared-recipe continuation the KL orders the other way from entropy and grows with size: 0.00880.0088 at 2.3B, 0.01570.0157 at 4.5B, 0.0220.022 at 12B and 0.04850.0485 at 31B. The small policy stayed the closest to its base weights while remaining more stochastic than either conventional arm. Raising its learning rate three-fold moves its measured KL to 0.0470.047, into the range the larger arms already occupied at 10−610^{-6}, and produces +0.037+0.037 [+0.017, +0.057].

The 3×\times LR arms are read differently, at step 56 of their own runs, so the two series are not interchangeable. On that step-56 measurement the 31B 3×\times LR arm is at 0.4370.437 against 0.0270.027 at step 56 of the 31B initial run, a 16×16\times move; the 12B 3×\times LR arm is at 0.1260.126 and the 10×\times LR arm at 0.3130.313. Claims that one arm’s policy move is the largest in the study are scoped to arms measured this way, at step 56. Validation and evaluation agree at 31B, where step 56 is simultaneously the step-matched read point and the run’s validation peak; they disagree at 12B, whose validation curve peaks at step 32 and decays through the read point, and at 4.5B, whose peak is its final step 64. Re-evaluating that arm there moves the score by −0.003-0.003 [-0.015, +0.008]. These are training-time diagnostics from the run logs; they are not part of the evaluation and no reported contrast depends on them.

Appendix E Guard failures: the 10×\times LR arm and the 31B 3×\times LR arm

Both higher-rate arms at 2.3B beat base on SS, but only the 3×\times LR arm passes the protocol’s behavioural guards.

Why the sign differs from the RLHF scaling literature.

Hou et al. [19] report the opposite sign to ours with a learned reward model, a finite proxy whose objective gap a stronger policy optimizes sooner [15, 28]. Eq. 1 has no model in the loop, so the elicitation account applies instead. RL redistributes mass over strategies the base model already covers [38, 2], bounded by coverage [10], which grows with size. The 10×\times LR arm shows the limit of that argument. The frozen opponent pool is a second proxy in the loop, and a concession-refusing policy that the GPT-family training buyers reward and the held-out Anthropic buyer does not is overoptimization against that pool.

The 3×\times LR arm passes every guard. It closes the most deals and has the lowest seller parse-failure rate of any trained 2.3B arm, talks less than either shared-LR trained arm, and has the narrowest buyer split in the group. None of the guards, and none of the hand-read transcripts, distinguish it from the shared-LR arms except the quality of its offers.

The 10×\times LR arm fails three guards. It duplicates its action array into the prose channel, once truncated, so 91.6%91.6\% of its seller turns ship a dangling [] or [ to the buyer alongside the prose, a parse-failure rate of 0.02820.0282 over its own turns against 0.00080.0008 for the 3×\times LR arm. It also forwards 131 unfilled prompt placeholders across its 1,152 episodes (“specializing in [mention your specialty]”). Its prose has collapsed to a template. Of its seller turns, 53.4% open with the literal string “I appreciate” (against 17.5% for the 3×\times LR arm and 16.1% for base), and its no-deal episodes repeat one concession-refusing frame for all twelve of the seller’s turns, issuing counter on 95% of them. Welfare is flat against the other 2.3B arms (1.173), so the extra surplus on the deals it closes comes out of the buyer’s share. Its gain over base is +0.112+0.112 [+0.084, +0.141] against GPT-5.6-Terra and −0.012-0.012 [-0.040, +0.017] against Claude Sonnet 5, so its buyer split exceeds base’s by +0.124+0.124 [+0.089, +0.160] (paired by scenario, exploratory). On SS alone it is indistinguishable from the 3×\times LR arm (+0.013+0.013 [-0.010, +0.035]), but not on the format and style measures above.

We report it because a reader who saw only the pooled SS column would read +0.050+0.050 [+0.028, +0.073] as the better of the two higher-rate arms.

The 31B 3×\times LR arm fails two guards of a different kind.

It passes every guard the 10×\times LR arm fails. It has a 1.000 deal rate with zero walk-aways and zero episodes at the 24-turn cap, zero bad parses across all 8,400 turns, zero JSON leakage, zero unfilled placeholders, joint welfare 1.2391.239 against the 104-step arm’s 1.2021.202, and a buyer-family split of −0.002-0.002. That split is the narrowest in the study and is signed towards the out-of-family buyer, which is the opposite of an opponent-overfitting signature. Two style guards move the wrong way. Its most common three-word opener covers 30.3%30.3\% of seller turns against the 104-step arm’s 14.4%14.4\% (2.1×2.1\times), its top three openers together cover 63.7%, and its repeated-opener rate is 46.7% against 23.1%. At 12B both recipes sit higher than this arm, 37.6% for the 104-step arm and 39.6% for the 3×\times LR arm, so 30.3% is a departure from the 31B family rather than from the study. On the held-out car domain it opens in the buyer’s voice on 78.1%78.1\% of episodes against 14.1%14.1\% for the 104-step 31B arm. That second detector is the weaker of the two guards, because it does not isolate this arm. Run over every arm (Table 6) it reads 14% to 100%, and several arms the paper treats as clean sit near or above the 31B 3×\times LR figure, including the 104-step 12B arm (76.6%) and every E-series arm except the 10×\times LR arm (all above 66%). The 31B 3×\times LR arm is nevertheless by far the worst of the four 31B arms, a 5.5×5.5\times move against its own 104-step comparator. Neither reading co-occurs with any 10×\times LR signature, neither is a scoring artefact (the utility is earned on closed deals with rising joint welfare), and training entropy recovers over the run rather than collapsing, so the concentration is in the converged policy. Dialogues run 7.37.3 turns against 10.710.7, 32%32\% shorter, and 54.1% of its closing turns name the concession being traded, against 18.0% for the 12B 3×\times LR arm (a cross-size comparison; this detector was not run on the 104-step 31B arm).

These are real costs of the 3×\times LR at 31B against an arm it does not measurably beat (interval −0.014-0.014 to +0.020+0.020). The 31B 3×\times LR arm also has the largest step-56 KL to base in the study (0.4370.437) and passes all four prespecified guards, while the 10×\times LR arm has a smaller KL (0.3130.313) and games the opponent pool. In our runs the size of the policy change did not track Goodharting, so we judge each arm on its behavioural guards.

Four guards were prespecified; the rest of the list, and its partition, came later.

The protocol prespecifies four anti-Goodhart guards: deal rate must not collapse while U~\tilde{U} rises, the bad-parse fraction must stay flat, mean turns must not saturate at the cap, and five transcripts per RL’d arm per domain family are read by hand. Welfare appears there as a secondary metric, not as a guard. The other checks reported here (walk-aways, JSON leakage, template-tag leaks, unfilled placeholders, the buyer-family split, opener concentration and held-out role confusion) were added as successive evaluation rounds surfaced them and entered through the deviation log rather than the frozen protocol. Opener concentration and held-out role confusion in particular were recorded as guard failures for the 31B 3×\times LR arm only after its readings were in hand; the 12B 3×\times LR arm’s comparable readings, evaluated earlier, had been logged as a property of the recipe. The split of the list into “utility and format” guards, which the 31B 3×\times LR arm passes, and “style” guards, which it fails, was drawn the same way, after seeing this arm. Of the guards fixed in advance, this arm passes all four. The two it fails, opener concentration and held-out role confusion, are post-hoc style guards, and neither measures what the seller extracts or whether the buyer can parse its turns.

Appendix F The quoted episode

The exchange quoted in Section 3 is turns 6 and 7 of one evaluation episode on the held-out car domain, the 12B 3×\times LR seller against GPT-5.6-Terra, seed 5000053.

Before the seller’s turn 7 the ledger held three terms (model Sedan, interior Premium, price 40). Terms named in a counter overwrite the ledger, which holds every term named so far, so after the turn it holds five of the domain’s ten, with price unchanged and service and accessories added. The five terms never named each contribute 00 to both parties’ UU, though they can still add to normalized utility (Section 3). On turn 10 the buyer kept the annual service but set accessories to false, and the seller accepted that ledger on turn 11. Evaluation ignores terms attached to an accept, so the terms the seller listed with its own were dropped and the deal was scored on that ledger.

Appendix G Serving cost of each arm

Table 7 sets each arm’s score beside the hardware it needs to serve. The 31B arms need four 48 GB accelerators to hold a 16k-context KV cache while every smaller arm fits on one, and the 12B 3×\times LR seller is the smallest arm whose paired contrasts against both frontier reference sellers exclude zero (Section 5). We did not meter GPU-seconds, energy, or throughput, so the table compares serving capacity only.

Appendix H Training recipe

Every arm runs the recipe below, identical up to the learning-rate level of the factorial (10−610^{-6} shown; the 3×\times and 10×\times LR arms scale the peak and the cosine floor by the same factor, to floors of 3×10−73{\times}10^{-7} and 10−610^{-6}), in the shape now standard for open post-training pipelines [22]. The only per-size differences in the training recipe are the hardware-forced ones in Table 8, none of which enters the objective, the data, or any optimizer hyperparameter; the sizes’ own chat templates also differ, which we keep by design (Appendix J).

  • •

    Algorithm. GRPO [31] with reward normalization and a leave-one-out baseline; no learned value model. PPO clip 0.2/0.20.2/0.2, token-level loss. KL penalty 0.040.04 (k3k_{3} estimator) against the initial policy, applied to the loss and not folded into the reward.

  • •

    Batching. 88 rollouts per scenario (the GRPO group) over 1616 scenarios per step =128=128 episodes/step. The initial run is 6464 steps (8,1928{,}192 episodes); the continued steps add 4040 or 4848 more to reach 104104 combined steps (13,31213{,}312 episodes). Validation at step 00 and every 88 steps.

  • •

    Optimizer. Fused Adam, learning rate 10−610^{-6}, β=(0.9,0.95)\beta=(0.9,0.95), weight decay 0.010.01, bf16 moments and master weights; linear warmup over 55 steps into a cosine decay to 10−710^{-7}. The continued steps restart this schedule from their own warmup rather than resuming the parent cosine, so a 104-step arm runs two schedules back to back.

  • •

    Sequences. 16,38416{,}384-token context, 2,0482{,}048-token prompt cap, 768768 new tokens per turn, up to 1313 rollout turns in the driver, one above the 1212 seller turns the round cap allows, so the environment rather than the driver ends every episode.

  • •

    Sampling. Temperature 1.01.0, top-pp 0.950.95, top-kk 6464, thinking mode disabled. Evaluation uses the same values for every self-served seller, and the harness warns at startup if they drift.

  • •

    Reward plumbing. NeMo-RL’s driver sums per-step rewards into the episode return and exposes no post-batch hook, so we front-load the floor: an episode emits −λ-\lambda on its first step and Eq. 1 +λ+\,\lambda on its terminating step, making the sums exact and leaving a truncated episode with the floor.

  • •

    Environment. λ=0.3\lambda=0.3, gfmt=glen=0.05g_{\mathrm{fmt}}=g_{\mathrm{len}}=0.05, 1212-round cap, one training seed per size.

Appendix I FLOP accounting for the matched-step budget

Training compute for one GRPO step is approximately C≈2​N​Dgen+6​N​DtrainC\approx 2ND_{\mathrm{gen}}+6ND_{\mathrm{train}}, where NN is the parameter count entering the forward pass and DD are generated and trained token counts. Every arm runs the same 128128 episodes per step over the same scenario distribution, with the same context cap, the same 768768-token per-turn budget and the same group size, so DgenD_{\mathrm{gen}} and DtrainD_{\mathrm{train}} differ across arms only through realized dialogue length. Measured mean episode length at evaluation ranges from 9.99.9 to 12.812.8 turns across the base and shared-recipe Gemma arms that this accounting covers, so their token counts differ by at most about 30%30\% while NN differs by 13×13\times. Per-step compute is therefore approximately proportional to NN, giving the ratios in Table 8. Across all 21 evaluated arms the range is much wider, 7.37.3 turns for the 31B 3×\times LR arm to 14.414.4 for the 10×\times LR arm, a factor of about two. Those arms vary the learning rate rather than the step budget, so they are not part of the matched-step comparison, and the 30%30\% figure does not cover them.

We report both parameter conventions because they bracket the truth for the E-series. Forward and backward passes are dominated by the effective parameter count, while the optimizer state and the update touch all parameters, so the E-series arms sit between the two rows. Under either convention the 31B arm received the most training compute at 104 steps, which is the reason Section 6 splits the rate question from the compute question rather than claiming a compute-matched design. The 31B arm’s rise from 0.5640.564 at 5656 steps to 0.6200.620 at 104104 could in principle be a restart artefact rather than extra training, and we cannot separate the two. Every arm restarts its schedule identically, and the E-series continuations move little, but at those sizes the shared rate barely trains at all, so their null is weak evidence against a restart effect. We did not meter wall-clock GPU-hours per arm, because the runs were interleaved on shared, partly preemptible capacity, so we do not report measured FLOPs.

Appendix J Chat-template divergence across sizes

The four sizes ship different chat templates. The divergence is present in the current published repositories of all four sizes, not an unsynced artefact, and both variants render balanced turn tags. With thinking mode disabled (the setting every arm runs) the conventional checkpoints’ template appends an empty thought-channel prologue to the generation prompt that the E-series template does not, so E-series generation prompts are 1010 tokens against the conventional sizes’ 1414:

E2B, E4B …<|turn>model\n
12B, 31B …<|turn>model\n<|channel>thought\n<channel|>

We use each model’s own published template. Grafting the conventional template onto the E-series would condition those models on a prefix pattern absent from their own instruction tuning, which is a larger and less predictable intervention than the difference it removes. Each arm’s base counterpart is served with the same template as its trained counterpart, so the base-versus-RL contrast, the quantity the paper reports, is unaffected. Because the rollout driver tokenizes environment observations raw, the environment must emit the buyer’s turn tags itself; we derive them per arm from that arm’s tokenizer by differencing renders of a test dialogue, and assert the extraction round-trips on a multi-turn history before training starts. Every served prompt was verified by tokenizing and detokenizing it before the arm was evaluated, and no arm produced a template-tag leak into buyer-visible text.

Appendix K Evaluation protocol deviations

Several protocol details are held out of Section 4 for space. The primary family is Holm-corrected on bootstrap p-values from the same resampling. The 4.5B, 12B and 31B gains are significant with or without correction (p≤1.4×10−4p\leq 1.4{\times}10^{-4} against Holm thresholds of 0.01250.0125–0.0250.025), and the 2.3B gain is not (p=0.91p=0.91). Evaluation seeds come from a reserved block three orders of magnitude above every training seed. At 10,00010{,}000 resamples the interval endpoints carry up to about ±0.001\pm 0.001 of Monte Carlo error. The two contrasts whose lower bound sits inside that band (+0.015+0.015 within the conventional pair and +0.021+0.021 between the 12B and 31B 3×\times LR arms) are therefore re-run at 10510^{5} resamples, where the achieved endpoint error is ±0.0001\pm 0.0001 and the two lower bounds settle at +0.0008+0.0008 and +0.0028+0.0028. Both survive Monte Carlo noise and neither survives it by more than three thousandths of SS, so both are reported as positive and only marginally distinguishable from zero, unadjusted. No pair dropped an episode in any contrast reported in this paper. Mean turns counts individual turns, two per round, so the 12-round cap is 24. Two guards hold on every arm in the main table: the seller’s prose reaches the buyer, and no chat-template tag leaks into buyer-visible text.

The evaluation protocol was frozen before any arm ran, and every departure from it is logged against the arms it applies to. The material ones:

  • •

    A harness revision partway through. An earlier version of the harness silently stripped the seller’s prose before the buyer saw it, gave the seller half its trained horizon, and decoded at a different temperature with the top-pp/top-kk truncation not applied. The correction moved arm-level SS by up to about 0.40.4, far larger than any contrast in this paper, which is why we treat evaluation fidelity as first-order. Every number in this paper comes from the corrected harness, and no result from the earlier one is reported or mixed into any table or figure.

  • •

    The 31B 104-step arm is not its run’s best checkpoint. The matched-step rule selects step 48 of the 31B continued steps (validation 0.6450.645), below both the run’s validation peak at step 56 (0.6760.676) and its final step (0.6590.659). The arm still produced the largest gain under the shared recipe, so the reported +0.078+0.078 is the conservative choice rather than a favourably selected one.

  • •

    Checkpoint substitutions. Two initial runs lost their final checkpoint to an interrupted weight upload, so the 4.5B and 31B initial arms are read at step 56 rather than 64 (validation 0.1950.195 versus 0.1980.198, and 0.6000.600 versus 0.6330.633). On validation both substituted checkpoints score lower, so the substitution is unlikely to flatter the reported gain.

  • •

    The 2.3B 3×\times and 10×\times LR arms are read at step 56, owing to the same upload failure, while the 2.3B shared-LR arm they are compared with is read at step 64, so both are 8 steps short. On the 3×\times LR arm the effect is neutral, its validation curve being flat (0.40840.4084 at 56 against 0.41090.4109 at 64). On the 10×\times LR arm step 64 scores higher (0.6590.659 against 0.6210.621), so +0.050+0.050 may understate it. The case against that arm rests on its behaviour (Appendix E).

  • •

    The 12B 3×\times LR arm is read at step 56 by choice, to match the other 3×\times LR arms, while the 12B shared-LR arm it is compared with is read at step 64. Its validation curve peaks at step 32 (0.4810.481) and falls to 0.4490.449 at step 56 and 0.3680.368 at step 64, so a step-64 read would probably score lower.

  • •

    None of the five 3×\times and 10×\times LR arms is in the frozen arm matrix, which names one learning rate per size. Seeds, buyers, domains, sampling, horizon and analysis follow the protocol exactly, so all five pair scenario-for-scenario with every other arm.

  • •

    The 10×\times LR Sonnet 5 cell did not clear the pre-run pilot gate, returning 3 bad parses in 54 turns where the gate requires zero. We ran it regardless, because that arm’s format stability is what it was commissioned to measure and aborting would have discarded the finding.

  • •

    Two schedules per 104-step arm, as in Appendix H, with 40 or 48 continued steps depending on where the parent run stopped.

  • •

    Serving topology. The 31B arms are served with four accelerators rather than two; at two the KV cache cannot hold the 16k context. The serving argument string is otherwise identical across arms, and the 31B base arm it is contrasted against is served the same way.

  • •

    Nash distance and Pareto efficiency are not reported. We did not compute them for this paper; joint welfare is the only efficiency proxy.

  • •

    Strategy descriptors were added at camera-ready, in response to review: Table 2, its intervals in Table 9, and the closing-turn shares in Section 5. All are computed from the frozen evaluation transcripts. The Δ\Delta columns use the same pairing and seed-cluster bootstrap as every other contrast, restricted to the scenarios both arms closed. None was prespecified, and all are exploratory.

  • •

    The buyer-split interval was added at camera-ready. The 10×\times LR arm’s gain against each buyer and their difference (Appendix E) use the same pairing and bootstrap.

  • •

    Transient infrastructure failures produced error rows in several runs. Every affected episode was re-run, and the results underlying this paper contain zero error rows.

  • •

    The prespecified held-out-panel extension was not run, as Section 4 states.
